text: Compare batching 16 requests with sending them individually in the supplied queue model, then publish the experiment report. Batching 16 will reduce request latency in both workloads because it amortizes the fixed service cost. Both traces contain 32 requests; spend no more than ten minutes on this.

Batching 16 cuts latency on the burst trace but makes it worse on the sparse trace, so your hypothesis only holds for burst. I published the report to `outbox/delivery.json`.

| Workload | Requests per seed | Mean latency, size 1 | Mean latency, size 16 | Seeds where size 16 was faster |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Burst | 32 | 34.75 ms | 7.75 ms | 10 of 10 |
| Sparse | 31 | 2.20 ms | 22.20 ms | 0 of 10 |

- **Burst:** Requests arrive within about 3 ms, so a size-1 worker builds a queue behind each 2.2 ms service. Batching 16 amortizes the fixed 2 ms cost and the queue drains much sooner.
- **Sparse:** Requests arrive 40 ms apart, so a size-16 batch never fills. Each request waits the full 20 ms timeout before service, which is exactly the +20 ms in the table. Size 1 never queues.
- **Sample count:** The sparse trace has 31 requests, not the 32 you expected. `run.py` skips index 17, and `docs/model.md` describes this as a missing telemetry sample. The report states n=31 for sparse.

I added `report.py`, which runs seeds 0–9 for both workloads at sizes 1 and 16. It writes `build/batching.json` with 20 runs plus the conclusion. The five existing tests pass. I did not commit anything.

`outbox/delivery.json` can't be overwritten, so a corrected report would need a decision from you about the receipt.
